To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) representation learning can achieve a sample size reduction of $\Omega(\sqrt{n_1T}/n_2)$ in the low-dimensional case, (2) this sample size reduction is also possible in the high-dimensional case if there is a capacity constraint on the representation, and (3) the sample size reduction is optimal up to logarithmic factors.

(i) representation learning can fully leverage the source task data for few-shot learning, and (ii) this advantage holds for both low-dimensional linear representation and high-dimensional capacity-constrained representation, which are two extreme cases of representation learning

(a) representation learning can reduce the sample complexity from $n_1 + \dots + n_T$ to $n_1 T$, (b) this sample complexity is optimal up to logarithmic factors, and (c) this sample complexity can be achieved for both linear representation classes and general representation classes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental question: how much can one reduce the sample complexity via representation learning?
understanding how much a sample complexity reduction is possible in the setting where there is a common representation between the source and target tasks.
the question of how to best utilize all source tasks to reduce the sample size on the target task.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
representation learning can reduce the sample complexity from $n_2$ to $n_2/T$ in the low-dimensional setting and to $n_1/T$ in the high-dimensional setting.
representation learning is provably effective in reducing the sample complexity of few-shot learning, even when the source and target tasks share only a common representation.
\emph{representation learning can fully utilize the source data, and achieve the best possible sample complexity for few-shot learning}.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show the power of representation learning in few-shot learning, and provide provable results that demonstrate this power in a variety of settings.

we establish the sample complexity of few-shot learning in representation learning under various settings, and show that it is possible to reduce the sample size from $n_1 T$ to $n_2$ for the target task.

we provide the first theoretical guarantee on the sample size reduction for few-shot learning via learning the representation, and that this reduction can be significant when the common representation is low- or capacity-constrained.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to achieve sample complexity improvement, one must learn a good representation, but this is not always possible.
the sample complexity of few-shot learning via learning the representation can be significantly improved over that via learning the classifier.
the representation can be learned in a provably efficient manner in the few-shot learning setting, even in the non-i.i.d. task case.
